# Form 27-B: Application for Continued Existence

## I.

The difference between Form 27-A and Form 27-B is a matter of three-sixteenths of a centimeter in the left margin and the relocation of Field 12 ("Declared Biomass of Applicant Civilization, Expressed in Standard Kelvin-Equivalents") from the second page to the third. Form 27-A was deprecated by the Office of Celestial Resource Allocation on a date that, when converted from Auditor chronological units to the Gregorian system, falls roughly on a Tuesday in the late Cretaceous. Form 27-B replaced it. The transition was announced in a memorandum that was, by all reasonable metrics, available.

No one on the colony ship *Kepler's Promise* had ever seen the memorandum.

This was understandable. The memorandum's distribution list encompassed all registered civilizations in the local galactic volume, but Earth had been "processed" — the Auditors' preferred term, carrying the same emotional valence as "filed," "sorted," or "recycled" — eleven years before the memorandum's issuance, and colony ships in transit were classified under Regulation 14-C as "pending entities," ineligible for direct correspondence until they established a fixed postal address, which they could not do because their destination was subject to a Habitation Permit that required, among other things, the correct completion of Form 27-B.

The circle, as even the most junior Auditor might have noted, was vicious. But junior Auditors did not note things. Noting was a function of the Division of Procedural Observation, which was three departments away and not accepting interdepartmental queries at this time.

The audit that discovered the discrepancy was itself routine. Every 6.4 years by the ship's clock, the onboard archive performed an automated reconciliation of all outgoing documentation against the Auditors' published standards — standards that were, in theory, accessible via a subspace reference beacon, though the beacon's signal had the character of a very old, very tired library that resented being asked questions. On this occasion, in the seventeenth year of the voyage, the reconciliation completed its cycle and produced a report that Navigator Chen found on her terminal at 0340 hours, between her second and third cups of coffee.

The report was nine hundred pages. Its executive summary was four words: TOTAL NON-COMPLIANCE. ALL SUBMISSIONS.

Chen stared at the screen. She set down her coffee. She picked it up again. She read the four words three more times to confirm that "total" meant total and "all" meant all. It did. They did. She called the Captain.

Captain Ade Okonkwo had been a systems engineer before the processing of Earth, and before that an officer in the Nigerian Navy, and before that a child who had once cried for two hours because a librarian told him his card was expired. He was a man who believed in the essential, if sometimes faltering, logic of organized systems. He had spent seventeen years maintaining that belief aboard a ship carrying four thousand human beings toward a planet they had been provisionally assigned by the very bureaucracy that had, with the same bland procedural efficiency, reduced their home world to its constituent atoms for "failure to meet minimum sustained-output thresholds as outlined in Resource Charter 11."

He arrived on the bridge in a bathrobe.

Chen showed him the report. He read the executive summary. He read it again. He opened the full report and scrolled through its pages — each one a meticulous comparison of their submitted forms against the current standard, each one annotated with the same red Auditor glyph that meant, approximately, "non-applicable, non-received, non-existent in the eyes of this office."

Seventeen years of petitions. Fuel-allotment requests that had kept the ship's engines burning. Census declarations that had affirmed, again and again, that humanity still existed and could be counted. Travel-clearance renewals filed at each checkpoint. All of it on Form 27-A. All of it, in the eyes of the Auditors' system, equivalent to blank paper.

The Captain gripped the edge of the navigation console. His knuckles went gray.

"They're telling me," he said, very quietly, "that everything we've sent them for seventeen years — every form, every filing, every single record of our existence — has been *wrong*?"

"Not wrong," Chen said. "Deprecated."

"We are four thousand people on a ship in the middle of nothing, traveling toward a world that a galactic filing office told us we could have, after that same filing office *composted our planet* — "

"Processed."

" — and now they're telling me the paperwork doesn't count because the *margin is wrong?*"

"The margin, and Field 12 is on the wrong page."

Captain Okonkwo released the console. He straightened. He breathed in through his nose, held it, and released a sound that was not a word in any human language but that carried, in its raw, guttural architecture, the full weight of a species' fury at the realization that the universe was not malicious, not indifferent, but *administrative.*

The sound echoed off the bridge walls. Chen waited. The navigation computer, mistaking the utterance for a vocal command, began plotting a course to nowhere in particular and had to be manually overridden.

By 0600, everyone who needed to know knew.

In the ship's archive — a climate-controlled room on Deck 7 that smelled of recycled air and the particular sorrow of organized paper — a woman named Dr. Yuna Sato sat at her desk and wept. Dr. Sato was the ship's chief records clerk, a title she had given herself because no one else had wanted it. She had personally overseen the preparation of every submission to the Auditors since Year One. She had hand-numbered each form in the upper right corner in a small, precise script, because the numbering system gave the submissions the appearance of sequence, of narrative, of a civilization that kept track of itself. She had told herself, during the worst nights — the nights when the ship's hull groaned in the void and four thousand people breathed recycled breath and the stars outside were not comforting but simply far away — that the forms were proof. Proof that they were here. Proof that they mattered enough to be counted.

She was not weeping because humanity might be doomed. She was weeping because she had numbered four hundred and thirty-seven forms in that small, precise script, and every single one of them was worthless, and the numbers she had written so carefully were just marks on deprecated paper, and no one — not human, not Auditor, not whatever incomprehensible system governed the cosmos — would ever read them.

Her assistant brought her tea. She held it and did not drink.

Three decks up, in the common area that served as a cafeteria, town hall, and arena for children's birthday parties, a woman named Gloria Paik heard the news from her neighbor, who had heard it from a water-treatment technician, who had heard it from Chen, who was on her fifth coffee and had stopped being careful about who she told.

Gloria was fifty-one years old. She had short gray-black hair, reading glasses she wore on a chain around her neck, and the particular posture of someone who has spent decades sitting in chairs designed to be sat in for no more than twenty minutes. Before the processing of Earth, she had worked for twenty-three years at the New Jersey Division of Motor Vehicles, first at the Trenton office and later at the regional annex in Ewing, where she had risen to the rank of Senior Processing Specialist III — a title that, on the organizational chart, sat between "Processing Specialist II" and "Assistant Supervisor," and that in practice meant she was the person other clerks came to when a form didn't make sense.

She had processed license renewals, title transfers, registration amendments, disability placards, vanity plate requests (which were their own special category of human sorrow), and a two-year backlog of unclaimed vehicle liens that she had cleared by working through an entire August while the air conditioning was broken, a feat for which she received a certificate of appreciation and a $25 gift card to a restaurant that had closed by the time she tried to use it.

She had been at the DMV on the day Earth was processed. Not at the moment of processing itself — that had happened at 3:47 a.m. Eastern Standard Time, and she had been asleep — but at 8:15 a.m., when she'd arrived at the Ewing office to find it still standing, because the Auditors' processing wave moved east to west and the northeastern seaboard had been, through a geographic accident that would haunt physicists for the remaining duration of human civilization, in a temporary shadow caused by the moon's orbital position. The Ewing annex, the Trenton DMV, a Wawa convenience store, and four thousand, two hundred and seventeen human beings in central New Jersey had survived the destruction of Earth because the moon was in the way.

Gloria had spent the next eleven hours in the Ewing office, processing the remaining customers in the queue, because the customers were there and the system was working and she did not yet understand what had happened. When she finally did understand — when the National Guard arrived and the sky turned the color of a form that has been left in the sun — she had locked the office, filed the day's paperwork in the outgoing bin, and walked to the evacuation point.

She had not cried. She had not screamed. She had, she would later realize, simply transferred her understanding of the universe from one filing system to another: the world was a place where forms were submitted, processed, sometimes rejected, and occasionally — if you were patient, if you understood the codes, if you did not make the mistake of believing the system owed you anything — approved.

Now she sat in the cafeteria of the *Kepler's Promise*, holding a cup of coffee that was not as bad as the coffee at the Ewing annex but was not good, and she listened to her neighbor explain that all of humanity's submissions had been on the wrong form.

"The margin's off," her neighbor said, the panic evident in her compressed shorthand. "Some field is on the wrong page. Everything's invalid. The Captain's — I think he broke something on the bridge."

Gloria took a sip of her coffee.

"It's just a form revision," she said.

"Gloria, they destroyed *Earth* over a paperwork issue — "

"They destroyed Earth over a resource threshold. This is a different issue. This is a versioning problem." She put down her coffee. "We were using 27-A?"

"I don't — yes, I think that's what — "

"And the current form is 27-B?"

"I don't know. Apparently."

Gloria nodded. She took off her reading glasses, cleaned them on her sleeve, and put them back on. She had once spent three weeks resolving a case in which a man's vehicle registration had been rejected fourteen times because the system required his middle name but his birth certificate didn't include one, and the "no middle name" code conflicted with a mandatory-field rule that had been implemented by a software update no one had documented. She had solved it by entering a single period in the middle-name field, which the system accepted as a character, and the man had wept at her window and called her a saint, and she had said, "Next, please."

"Okay," Gloria said. "So we refile."

---

## II.

The process by which Gloria Paik was designated as humanity's advocate to the Auditor system was, itself, a notable artifact of bureaucratic entropy.

The Captain convened an emergency council. The emergency council determined that a subcommittee was needed. The subcommittee met four times, produced a report recommending the formation of a task force, and dissolved itself due to a quorum dispute. The task force, once formed, spent two weeks debating whether humanity's representative should be a diplomat, a scientist, a philosopher, or a lawyer, and concluded, after a particularly heated session in which three people resigned and one proposed sending the ship's cat, that the representative should be someone with "demonstrated expertise in navigating complex administrative systems."

Dr. Sato, who had stopped weeping and started cross-referencing every Auditor regulation she could pull from the subspace beacon, nominated Gloria. The Captain objected, on the grounds that the survival of the human species should not rest on "a DMV employee from New Jersey." Gloria, who was present, pointed out that she was a *Senior Processing Specialist III* from New Jersey, and that moreover, the Captain's proposed alternative — a retired international trade lawyer who had once negotiated a tariff agreement with the European Union — had never, to Gloria's knowledge, successfully renewed a driver's license without an appointment.

The trade lawyer conceded the point.

Gloria was designated. The paperwork confirming her designation took five days to process internally, because the ship's own administrative system required two signatures that could only be obtained during office hours, and office hours had been reduced due to the energy-conservation protocols that were themselves the subject of one of the deprecated Form 27-A submissions. Gloria signed the forms, collected her files, and reported to the Communications Bay, where Dr. Sato had determined that the Auditor subspace beacon could be used, if properly manipulated, to request a "Direct Advocate Interface" — teleportation, more or less, to an Auditor intake facility.

"Do we know what happens there?" Gloria asked.

"No," said Dr. Sato.

"Do we know if it's safe?"

"The beacon describes it as 'a standard processing environment.'"

Gloria considered this. She had spent twenty-three years in standard processing environments.

"I'll need my briefcase," she said.

The transportation itself was unremarkable from Gloria's perspective — a brief sensation of being collated, as though her atoms were being alphabetized — and then she was somewhere else.

The waiting room was precisely a waiting room.

This was, Gloria would later reflect, both its most disorienting and most reassuring quality. The floor was a material that was not linoleum but behaved like linoleum: faintly glossy, vaguely resistant to scuffing, the color of institutional resignation. The walls existed in the way that waiting-room walls always exist — as boundaries that neither invite nor repel attention, merely confirming that you are inside rather than outside. The lighting had no visible source. It simply was, in the way that waiting-room lighting is always simply *is*: bright enough to read forms, dim enough to erode your sense of how long you've been reading them.

There were chairs. They were almost comfortable. They were the exact chairs of every waiting room Gloria had ever known — chairs that had been designed by someone who understood the concept of sitting but had perhaps never done it recreationally. They supported the body without welcoming it. They permitted rest without encouraging it. They were, in their profound ergonomic ambivalence, the most familiar objects Gloria had encountered since leaving Earth.

She sat down. The chair accepted her with the particular lack of enthusiasm she had expected.

To her left, a number-dispensing kiosk rose from the floor like a small, apologetic monument. It was made of a material that might have been metal or might have been solidified protocol — Gloria did not examine it too closely, on the principle that some things in administrative facilities are best used without being understood. She pulled a ticket. The ticket was printed with a symbol that existed in no human language, a glyph that suggested, if you tilted your head and squinted, something between "G" and "7012" and a small, resigned sigh. She would come to think of it as G-7012. The kiosk did not object.

She sat back down with her ticket and opened her briefcase.

The briefcase was the same one she had carried to the Ewing annex every day for eleven years. It was brown, scuffed at the corners, and exactly the right size for a standard stack of forms plus one emergency pen, two backup pens, a small stapler, a package of binder clips, and a sleeve of color-coded filing tabs — green for census, yellow for fuel, red for travel, blue for miscellaneous. She had repacked it with the 27-B refiled versions of every submission humanity had made, retyped by Dr. Sato's team over seventy-two sleepless hours and checked twice by Gloria against the subspace beacon's published field requirements. Four hundred and thirty-seven forms. Dr. Sato had not hand-numbered these — Gloria had told her not to, not because the numbers didn't matter, but because she wanted the new forms to look like what they were: clean, correct, ready.

She organized them by category. Green tabs, yellow tabs, red tabs, blue tabs. She aligned the edges. She placed them in her lap.

Then she looked up, and she saw the others.

They filled the waiting room in rows and clusters and solitary nodes of patience that extended in every direction farther than the space should have permitted. The room was not large — it had the dimensions of a mid-sized post office — and yet it contained multitudes, in the way that bureaucratic spaces have always contained multitudes: by simply adding more chairs.

Nearest to Gloria, in a cluster of seats that might have been Row F, a delegation of beings that resembled tall, thin stalks of wheat — if wheat had been grown in an environment of pure mathematics
